title: Praying for others by name
hookLine: Christians pray for people by name, trusting God hears

lines: AARON AND HUR HOLD THEM UP.
cards: Somebody texts you: please pray for my dad, surgery Thursday. Maybe you pray; maybe you don't know what to do with that. The request is old, and Exodus has a picture of it.
In a battle, Moses stands on a hill above Israel with his arms raised. While his hands are up, the story says, Israel prevails; when they drop, Israel loses ground. Arms get heavy.
So his brother Aaron and a man named Hur sit Moses on a stone and hold his arms up, one on each side, until sunset. In the King James, "Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands."
Some Christian readers see in that picture prayer for someone else.

teach.b: Intercession comes from Latin, to go between: stepping in for someone, standing between them and what they're facing, and bringing them before God. The New Testament puts it on the list early.
Paul writes to Timothy: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men."

teach.h: FIRST OF ALL, FOR ALL PEOPLE.
teach.b: First of all, for all people. The Bible is full of people praying for others. Abraham bargains with God over a whole city.

Jesus tells Peter, before Peter's worst night, that he has prayed for him, that his faith would not fail. On the cross, Luke says, Jesus prays: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the names.
Paul's letters are crowded with them, and he tells his friends he remembers them in his prayers.
A name makes it real: not the sick in general, but Marta, in room four. Churches do it differently.

In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran services, the prayers of the people bring the sick, the grieving and the world before God. In Orthodox liturgy, the priest reads out names of the living and the departed.
Many evangelical churches run prayer chains, a phone tree praying for whoever needs it this week.
Catholics and Orthodox Christians also ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend; many Protestants ask only God, and their friends still on earth.

All share James's plain instruction: "pray one for another." Nobody claims to know exactly how it works. Christians say God hears, and that holding someone up changes something, often in the one who holds.

how: Christians pray for others by name in private prayer and in church: the prayers of the people in many liturgies, the reading of names in Orthodox services, and prayer lists and prayer chains in many Protestant churches.

o: a short break in the middle of a service
praying for someone else, on their behalf
a plea to God for your own forgiveness

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: first of all, for all people

s: intercession means praying only for yourself
it means stepping between: praying for someone else.
in Exodus, two men hold up Moses's arms until sunset
Aaron and Hur, one on each side.
every church prays for others the same way
prayers of the people, names read at the Orthodox liturgy, prayer chains: many ways, one practice.

games.q: you're Aaron. the battle is below, and your brother's arms are shaking and starting to drop. what do you do?
o: take the staff and hold it up yourself.
sit him on a stone and hold his arms up.
tell him to rest; the battle will be fine.
games.why: Aaron and Hur sit Moses on a stone and hold his hands steady until sunset. they don't replace him. they hold him up.

practice: Let three names come, one at a time: someone struggling right now, someone you love and don't worry about, and someone difficult; that one's harder, so just the name is enough.
If you pray, hold each up to God, in a sentence or in silence; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Intercession: praying for someone else, by name, bringing them before God.

orig.note: Greek, in 1 Timothy 2:1: intercession, a word for coming to someone on another's behalf.

carryVoice: Your line: hold them up. Tomorrow, a psalm that asks how long. See you then.
